c.tagline: Kurdish heartland of western Iran, guarded by Sassanid rock reliefs and ancient inscriptions.

taxi.fareNote: Foreign bank cards do not work anywhere in Iran, so carry rials in cash for taxis. The Snapp and Tapsi apps give fixed in-app prices; shared and private street taxis are negotiated before you ride.

emergency.note: Dial 110 for police and 115 for the emergency medical/ambulance service; 125 reaches the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: No no-go areas in the city, but stay clear of the immediate Iraq border zone in the west of the province.

hood_desc: The bustling old core around Shahrdari (Municipality) Square and the covered Grand Bazaar, with the beautiful Tekyeh Moaven ol-Molk tilework nearby; the walkable heart for markets, mosques, and street food.
The green northeastern district built around the Taq-e Bostan Sassanid rock reliefs and their spring-fed pool, ringed by teahouses and kebab restaurants; scenic and sight-focused.
The modern business, shopping, and hotel district along Shahid Kishvari Boulevard near the Velayat Bridge, home to the city's five-star Parsian hotel and its main commercial towers.

water.note: Tap is treated but visitors usually drink bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; taxis and the Snapp/Tapsi apps cover late-night trips.
transit.note: Kermanshah has no metro; public transport is city buses plus a dense network of shared and private taxis, supplemented by the Snapp and Tapsi ride-hailing apps.
transit.pay: Bus and taxi fares are paid in cash (rials) — foreign cards are useless in Iran. Ride-hailing apps are prepaid in-app or settled in cash to the driver.

bus: Intercity coaches to Tehran, Hamadan, and Sanandaj
train: Limited weekly rail service to Tehran

transit.m: Snapp or Tapsi ride-hail from the terminal

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up is common, and small amounts may be politely refused at first as part of taarof courtesy.

food.name: Dande kabab
food.desc: Kermanshah's signature dish: a wide slab of lamb ribs basted with saffron, tomato and lemon, grilled slowly until the fat crisps.

places.name: Heidari Restaurant
places.note: The name locals give first for dande kabab, set among the rib grills lining the Taq-e Bostan gardens.

places.name: Chelcheleh Restaurant
places.note: Long-running city-centre kababi with a full Kermanshahi menu and reliable service for visitors.

places.name: Shaili International Restaurant
places.note: Smarter sit-down option often recommended to travellers for ribs and rice dishes.

food.name: Khoresh-e khalal
food.desc: Slow-cooked lamb stew with slivered almonds, barberries and saffron; a Kermanshahi banquet dish, usually served over steamed rice.

places.name: Shaili International Restaurant
places.note: One of the few sit-down places that keeps this labour-intensive stew on the daily menu.

places.name: Chelcheleh Restaurant
places.note: Regional stews alongside the grills; ask what is cooking that day, as stews rotate.

places.name: Taq-e Bostan garden restaurants
places.note: Cluster of family restaurants below the rock reliefs where khalal appears at weekends and feasts.

food.name: Nan-e berenji
food.desc: Pale, crumbly rice-flour cookies scented with cardamom and rosewater, stamped with a pattern; the classic edible souvenir of Kermanshah.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik (Dark Bazaar) sweet shops
places.note: Historic covered bazaar where confectioners sell nan-e berenji and kak by the boxed kilo.

places.name: Javanshir Bazaar confectioners
places.note: Row of traditional shirini shops turning out fresh batches through the day.

places.name: Modarres Street pastry shops
places.note: Modern confectioners on the main shopping street with gift-wrapped tins.

food.name: Roghan-e Kermanshahi
food.desc: Prized nomadic sheep-milk clarified butter with a deep golden colour; drizzled over rice, stews and breakfast eggs across the province.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik dairy stalls
places.note: Traders sell the real village ghee by weight; smell and colour are the local quality test.

places.name: Javanshir Bazaar
places.note: Tins and jars of roghan sold beside honey and nuts, a standard Kermanshah gift.

places.name: Heidari Restaurant
places.note: Easiest way to taste it cooked, spooned over rice served with the ribs.

food.name: Kalaneh
food.desc: Kurdish flatbread stuffed with mountains of chopped spring herbs and leeks, griddled in ghee and torn apart to share.

places.name: Taq-e Bostan garden restaurants
places.note: Griddled to order as a starter at the open-air places by the springs.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik bakeries
places.note: Morning bakers sell herb-stuffed breads hot off the plate for a few tomans.

places.name: Chelcheleh Restaurant
places.note: Appears with the bread and mezze course at this city-centre standby.

food.name: Ash-e Kermanshahi
food.desc: Thick herb, bean and noodle soup finished with fried mint and whey; sold from steaming cauldrons, especially in the cold months.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik ash stalls
places.note: Cauldron cooks ladle ash into bowls from mid-morning; busiest in winter.

places.name: Javanshir Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Cheap standing-room bowls with kashk stirred through, popular with market workers.

places.name: Chelcheleh Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down version of the soup if you would rather have a table.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted, lightly fizzy yoghurt drink flecked with dried mint; the standard partner to grilled lamb and the antidote to rich ghee.

places.name: Heidari Restaurant
places.note: House doogh in chilled jugs, poured throughout the rib feast.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik dairy stalls
places.note: Village-made doogh sold by the bottle beside the ghee and cheese.

places.name: Chelcheleh Restaurant
places.note: Reliable cold doogh with every kebab order in the centre.

food.name: Chai with nabat
food.desc: Strong black tea in a slim estekan glass, sweetened with a saffron rock-sugar stick; the all-day social ritual of the city.

places.name: Taq-e Bostan teahouses
places.note: Terraces facing the Sasanian reliefs and spring pools, best in the late afternoon.

places.name: Bazar-e Tarik teahouses
places.note: Old vaulted chai khanehs tucked into the bazaar lanes, samovar always on.

places.name: Javanshir Bazaar tea stalls
places.note: Quick glass with a stick of nabat between shopping stops.

landmarks: Taq-e Bostan
Sassanid kings carved triumphant rock reliefs and grottoes into this cliffside above a spring-fed pool, including the celebrated armored knight Khosrow II.
Tekyeh Moaven ol-Molk
A Qajar-era Shiite mourning house adorned with Iran's most extraordinary painted tilework, depicting Karbala battles, kings and even biblical scenes.
Kermanshah Traditional Bazaar (Tarikeh Bazaar)
One of Iran's liveliest provincial bazaars winds through Qajar-era arcades fragrant with kermanshahi oil, sweets and Kurdish handicrafts.
Emad od-Dowleh Mosque
This elegant Qajar Friday mosque at the bazaar's heart features a famed silver-and-gold door and finely tiled courtyard iwans.
Tekyeh Biglar Beygi
A dazzling mirror-work ceremonial hall from the Qajar era, its shattered-glass dome interior now hosts a calligraphy museum.
Sarab-e Niloufar
A spring-fed pond famous for its summer carpet of blooming lotus flowers, a beloved picnic escape twenty minutes from downtown Kermanshah.
Shafei Mosque
A Sunni mosque near the old Tarikeh bazaar, built in 1945 in Ottoman-influenced style with five domes, ornate stucco, and sunlit hypostyle prayer halls.
Jameh Mosque of Kermanshah
The city's historic Friday mosque near the old bazaar quarter, its brick minarets and prayer hall reflecting centuries of rebuilding across Safavid, Zand and Qajar rule.
Dowlatshah Mosque
A Qajar-era mosque in Kermanshah's old quarter, its tiled portal and courtyard shabestan preserving the understated brick-and-tile style of the city's nineteenth-century religious architecture.
Kuhestan Park
A large hillside park in northern Kermanshah with man-made waterfalls, fountains, and shaded lawns, plus a memorial to unknown soldiers overlooking the city below.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international passenger trains - the line toward the Iraqi border at Khosravi carries no scheduled cross-border service. Kermanshah has a limited rail link east toward Tehran taking about 10 hours; the coach is quicker. Book through a hotel or agent, as Raja's site does not accept foreign cards.

intl.to: Najaf & Karbala (Iraq) - via the Khosravi border, mainly around pilgrimage seasons
intl.op: Iranian coach operators — tickets at the Kermanshah terminal, no online booking

bus.note: Kermanshah is a staging point for pilgrims crossing to the Iraqi shrine cities, and coach traffic through the Khosravi border swells enormously around Arbaeen, when the route can be overwhelmed. Outside those weeks services are sporadic - check locally. Domestic VIP coaches reach Tehran in about 7 hours and Hamadan in 3; buy at the terminal in cash.

ferry.note: Kermanshah is inland in the western Zagros with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.blurb: UNESCO-listed cliff carved with Darius the Great's trilingual inscription, ~30 km east toward Hamadan.
half.name: Bisotun

full.blurb: Colossal stone columns of an ancient temple often linked to the goddess Anahita, ~90 km toward Hamadan.
full.name: Anahita Temple, Kangavar

full.blurb: One of Asia's longest water caves, explored by boat in the mountains west of the city.
full.name: Quri Qaleh Cave
